title: Jentel Manufacturing (June 2010 TCC) Tax Court Ruling
subject: Earlier Tax Court SR&ED proceeding involving Jentel Manufacturing Ltd.'s precision manufacturing claims.
summary: Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261, heard June 2010; aff'd 2011 FCA 355) is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision affecting Canadian manufacturers claiming experimental development. The Court denied Jentel's 2005 claim, holding that systematic testing and contemporaneous records cannot overcome the absence of technological uncertainty where work amounts to routine engineering.
metaDescription: Examine the June 2010 Tax Court of Canada ruling for Jentel Manufacturing regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit litigation.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural History and Jurisdictional Context

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, Docket 2008-3875(IT)G, heard in Calgary, Alberta, on June 11, 2010, with formal Reasons for Judgment rendered by the Honourable Justice Steven K. D'Arcy on May 11, 2011 (cited as 2011 TCC 261), stands as a foundational precedent in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax jurisprudence. The trial judgment was subsequently affirmed unanimously by the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) on December 15, 2011 (cited as 2011 FCA 355, Docket A-222-11, reasons delivered by Justice Carolyn Layden-Stevenson). Within the Canadian federal tax architecture, Jentel represents a critical demarcation point between systematic commercial product development and eligible experimental development under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the Act).

The litigation arose after the Minister of National Revenue (the Minister), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), issued a Notice of Reassessment disallowing SR&ED expenditure claims and associated Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) claimed by Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. (the Appellant) for its fiscal and taxation year ended October 31, 2005. The central legal question before the Tax Court of Canada was whether the expenditures incurred by the Appellant in overhauling its proprietary storage product constituted expenditures on SR&ED within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the Act, such that they were qualified SR&ED expenditures.
The Taxpayer's Technical Operations and the 2005 SR&ED Claim

Having commenced commercial operations in the fall of 1993, Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. operated as an industrial plastic sheet thermoformer developing and manufacturing engineered thermoformed plastic products for both consumer and industrial markets. While the company performed a significant amount of custom work for third parties—making such things as enclosures, displays, and tote bins—the company also manufactured and marketed a proprietary small-parts storage system designated as "Multi-Bins". In its original iteration, developed in prior fiscal years, the Multi-Bins assembly comprised a plastic back panel onto which thermoformed plastic bin fronts were mechanically fastened using screws arranged in horizontal rows. The legacy system could be mounted on walls or configured as a free-standing floor unit to store hardware and small components at manufacturing workstations, in maintenance stores, and in home workshops.

During the 2005 fiscal year, Jentel initiated a comprehensive engineering overhaul of the Multi-Bins product line. The overarching commercial and operational mandate of the project was to re-engineer the existing product into a smaller, substantially lighter storage assembly that required reduced shop-floor labour to manufacture, simplified end-user installation, and lowered energy consumption during freight transport. As stipulated in the Statement of Agreed Facts (SAF) filed jointly by counsel at trial, Jentel structured the 2005 overhaul around five specific, measurable design objectives: increasing the volumetric storage capacity of the system to 20 cubic feet per square metre of floor footprint (representing double the prevailing industry standard); enabling each individual bin front to support a load of 100 pounds; developing a new "snap-fit" design for the bin fronts to eliminate the need for fasteners; introducing system-wide geometric modularity; and replacing non-recyclable structural plastics, such as acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), with recyclable ones, such as polypropylene.

In its regulatory filings submitted to the CRA on Form T661, Jentel partitioned its fiscal 2005 experimental activities into four distinct component sub-projects: Bin Front and Back Panels, Stands, Sliders, and Dividers. Across all four categories, the SAF records that the Appellant conducted tests or design trials and that contemporaneous records of this work were kept; the SAF further states that the work on the Bin Front and Back Panels and on the Stands was performed in a systematic manner.

cells: Bin Front and Back Panels

Performed a series of tests under a variety of moulding conditions using at least eight different plastic materials: PETG, PVC, acrylic, ABS, styrene, Lexan (polycarbonate), HDPE, and polyethylene; for two of those materials (ABS and HDPE), further testing was carried out using varying thicknesses of material to determine strength characteristics. Mr. Hahn testified that a so-called "heat sink" was used while thermoforming, which he acknowledged was merely plug-assist forming technology that had been in use for quite some time.
The SAF records no specific outcome for these tests; it states that contemporaneous records of this work were kept and that the work was performed in a systematic manner.
Stands

Constructed prototype structural stands using different materials for some of the components: wood, a wood/plastic combination, plastic, and aluminum, testing each against defined design and manufacturing criteria.
Load testing showed that aluminum was the best suited for the application; the SAF states that contemporaneous records were kept and that this work was performed in a systematic manner.
Sliders
Designed, fabricated, and mechanically tested numerous geometric shapes and structural forms of sliding mechanisms for the storage bins.
None of the prototype slider geometries operated satisfactorily; contemporaneous records of the trials were maintained.
Dividers

Executed moulding trials to form a retention groove inside the front panel of the Multi-Bins to receive and secure an internal partition divider. Tested three distinct moulds fabricated from different casting materials alongside multiple iterations of groove geometry.
Each of Jentel's attempts to create a groove in the part that could be manufactured on a consistent basis failed; contemporaneous records of this work were kept.

body.text: The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister denied Jentel's claim on the basis that the work performed did not meet the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Act; at trial, the Crown called Mr. Phillip Leong, a research technology advisor (RTA) for the CRA, as a witness. In the Reply to the Notice of Appeal, the Crown pleaded that the Minister's reassessment rested on core factual assumptions, notably paragraph 13(l), which posited that the Appellant had failed to demonstrate a systematic investigation through experiment or analysis performed to resolve any scientific or technical uncertainties that may have arisen through the development of the Multi-Bins or its component parts. In paragraph 13(m) of the Reply, the Minister further assumed that the work performed by the Appellant in its development of the product or its component parts was in line with standard product development and did not represent scientific or technical advancement.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

The eligibility of R&D activities in Canada is governed by the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set forth in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (which replaced and codified the regulatory criteria formerly housed in section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations), working in tandem with section 37 (which governs the deduction of qualified SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada) and subsections 127(5) and 127(9) (which govern the calculation and claiming of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits). In Jentel, the statutory inquiry centred specifically on paragraph (c) of the subsection 248(1) definition, which defines experimental development as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that is undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

To operationalize the statutory text of subsection 248(1), Canadian courts apply the five-part jurisprudential framework originally articulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC), and subsequently adopted as binding appellate law by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132 (FCA), and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (at paragraph 17). Justice D'Arcy anchored his legal analysis on the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, as summarized by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies at paragraph 17: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.
The Court's Final Holding

Justice D'Arcy dismissed Jentel's appeal in its entirety and awarded costs to the Crown. In reaching this disposition, the Tax Court made a critical preliminary evidentiary ruling: while finding both the Appellant's president (Mr. Ralph Hahn) and the CRA's RTA (Mr. Phillip Leong) to be credible witnesses, the Court placed no weight on the testimony of the CRA's RTA because, in the Court's view, most of his evidence was opinion evidence.

Notwithstanding the absence of weight given to the Crown's technical witness and the Crown's stipulation in the SAF that Jentel had performed tests in a "systematic manner" while keeping "contemporaneous records," Justice D'Arcy held that the Appellant failed at the threshold stage of the Northwest Hydraulic test. Relying on the SAF and on Mr. Hahn's own testimony, the Court concluded that Jentel's work involved using existing manufacturing processes (thermoforming and injection moulding, which the Court described as well-known) and existing materials in an attempt to improve its existing product, which involved routine engineering and standard procedures—Mr. Hahn was simply describing the use of existing manufacturing processes in an attempt to build a better product while controlling manufacturing costs. The Court found that there was no evidence that any of the work involved technological risk or uncertainty, and that the Appellant failed to establish a prima facie case that it was attempting technological advancement, so the Minister's assumptions were not demolished and the reassessment was left undisturbed. On appeal, the Federal Court of Appeal (2011 FCA 355) affirmed the judgment with costs, holding that the trial judge committed no error of law in articulating the statutory test and no palpable and overriding error in concluding that Jentel's evidence demonstrated only routine engineering.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures
Conflation of Commercial Product Specifications with Technological Uncertainty

The primary substantive defect that invalidated Jentel's claim was the fundamental conflation of ambitious commercial design specifications with "technological risk or uncertainty" under subsection 248(1) of the Act. In preparing its claim, the Appellant framed its project around five quantitative and functional targets: doubling the storage density to 20 cubic feet per square metre, achieving a 100-pound bin-front load rating, replacing mechanical screws with a snap-fit joint, introducing modularity, and substituting recyclable polypropylene for non-recyclable ABS. While these objectives represented formidable industrial design and cost-optimization challenges for a commercial product overhaul, Canadian tax law draws a rigid distinction between a product or business uncertainty (whether a product with desired commercial attributes can be fabricated within market cost constraints) and a technological uncertainty (whether a scientific or technological capability gap prevents a competent professional from achieving an objective using available engineering knowledge).

Quoting paragraph 16 of Justice Bowman's seminal decision in Northwest Hydraulic, Justice D'Arcy emphasized that implicit in the term "technological risk or uncertainty" is the requirement that the uncertainty cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. If the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures, there is no technological uncertainty in this context; Justice Bowman also clarified that he was not referring to the mere doubt that may exist, whenever a problem is identified, concerning the way in which it will be solved. Applying this standard, Justice D'Arcy found that there was no evidence before him that any of Jentel's work involved technological risk or uncertainty (paragraph 16); nothing in the evidence explained why a competent professional using routine engineering or standard procedures could not achieve the 100-pound load target or a snap-fit geometry using polypropylene. Instead, the SAF framed the work around commercial performance objectives, and the Court concluded that those measurable objectives were pursued through routine engineering rather than through an attempt to achieve technological advancement.
Parametric Material Screening and Routine Engineering in Thermoforming

A detailed examination of the technical evidence adduced by Jentel's president, Mr. Hahn, reveals why the Tax Court classified all four work categories as "routine engineering or standard procedures"—defined by the Court as techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the relevant field. During trial, Mr. Hahn explained that in plastic sheet thermoforming, third-party extruders heat plastic resin and extrude it into a sheet, the thermoformer specifies the required gauge, size, and type of plastic, and the thermoformer then forms the sheet into shapes using moulds, vacuums, and air pressure; he also noted that extrusion changes the properties of the resin, so the actual specifications of the extruded sheet are not known. To overhaul the Multi-Bins panels, Jentel tested at least eight different plastic materials—PETG, PVC, acrylic, ABS, styrene, Lexan, HDPE, and polyethylene—under a variety of moulding conditions, with further testing at varying thicknesses for two of them (ABS and HDPE). Similarly, for the Stands, Jentel built prototypes out of wood, wood/plastic combinations, plastic, and aluminum before concluding via load testing that aluminum was optimal.

Justice D'Arcy stated at paragraph 24 of the judgment that, with respect to the use of different types of plastic resin or materials, he failed to see how this constituted SR&ED. In materials engineering, comparative material selection (screening known materials with published mechanical properties against functional design criteria) and parametric machine tuning (adjusting heating zones, dwell times, or vacuum pressure on a thermoforming press) are the quintessential functions of routine product engineering. Even where Jentel encountered repeated failures—such as none of the sliders working satisfactorily and every attempt, using three moulds of different casting materials, failing to produce a divider groove that could be manufactured on a consistent basis—the Court did not treat those failures as evidence of technological risk or uncertainty; it made no finding as to their cause and held that there was no evidence that any of the work involved technological risk or uncertainty.

This technical deficiency was fatally compounded by Mr. Hahn's testimony regarding the company's use of a "heat sink" during the thermoforming of the panels. When thermoforming semi-crystalline polymers such as polypropylene, plastic resins exhibit a narrow thermoforming temperature window and low melt strength (excessive sheet sag) compared to amorphous plastics like ABS. At trial, Mr. Hahn implied that Jentel's use of a "heat sink" while thermoforming constituted experimental development. However, as Mr. Hahn himself stated during his testimony, the so-called heat sink was merely plug-assist forming technology that had "been out there for quite some time". Justice D'Arcy relied on this statement at paragraph 23, finding that the use of the heat sink also appeared to be routine engineering or use of standard procedures. More broadly, the Court characterized Mr. Hahn's evidence as describing the use of existing manufacturing processes in an attempt to build a better product while controlling manufacturing costs, with no evidence of an attempt to achieve a technological advancement.
The Strategic Paradox of the Statement of Agreed Facts (SAF)

From a tax litigation perspective, Jentel presents a striking cautionary lesson regarding reliance on an SAF. In many unsuccessful SR&ED appeals before the Tax Court of Canada, taxpayers lose because they lack contemporaneous documentation (Criterion 5) or because their testing was chaotic, unrecorded "trial and error" rather than a systematic investigation (Criterion 3). In Jentel, remarkably, the Crown agreed in the SAF that the work on the Bin Front and Back Panels and on the Stands "was performed in a systematic manner" (SAF paragraphs 11(d) and 12(e)) and that "contemporaneous records of this work were kept" for all four work areas (SAF paragraphs 11(c), 12(d), 13(c), and 14(d)).

Academic and legal commentary on Jentel cautions against assuming that, if the Crown stipulates that testing was systematic and contemporaneously documented, eligibility follows almost automatically; notably, however, the Tax Court's reasons record that Jentel's closing argument rested principally on Mr. Hahn's testimony and the Hickman Motors burden-shifting principle (paragraph 25) rather than on the SAF admissions. Justice D'Arcy's reasons show why such an assumption is misplaced: he found no evidence of technological risk or uncertainty and no prima facie case of an attempt to achieve technological advancement, and, as the Federal Court of Appeal later noted (2011 FCA 355, paragraph 6), his finding on the first criterion was dispositive, so it was unnecessary for him to address the remaining criteria. A taxpayer can execute a highly disciplined, systematic series of comparative tests and maintain meticulous contemporaneous logs, yet still be engaged in 100% routine engineering if the tests are not governed by a scientific hypothesis (Criterion 2) specifically formulated to resolve a genuine technological uncertainty. Moreover, the evidence described in the reasons consisted of the SAF and the testimony of two witnesses (Mr. Hahn and Mr. Leong); the Court found that this evidence, particularly the SAF and Mr. Hahn's testimony, demonstrated work involving routine engineering and standard procedures, and did not establish a prima facie case that the work was undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement.
Evidentiary Burden, Hickman Motors, and Witness Qualification Dynamics

The procedural climax of the Jentel trial revolved around the shifting burden of proof in Canadian tax litigation under the Supreme Court of Canada's doctrine in Hickman Motors Ltd. v. Canada, [1997] 2 S.C.R. 336 (at paragraphs 92–94). In Canadian tax appeals, the Minister's factual assumptions pleaded in the Reply are presumed to be true; the initial onus rests on the taxpayer to "demolish" those assumptions by making out at least a prima facie case. Once the taxpayer establishes a prima facie case, the evidentiary burden shifts to the Crown to rebut the taxpayer's evidence and prove the Minister's assumptions on a balance of probabilities.

At trial, the Crown called CRA RTA Phillip Leong as its sole witness. However, Justice D'Arcy placed no weight on Mr. Leong's testimony because, in his view, most of Mr. Leong's evidence was opinion evidence; the reasons do not indicate that Mr. Leong was tendered or qualified as an expert witness. Counsel for Jentel submitted in closing argument (quoted at paragraph 25 of the TCC reasons, from paragraph 26 of the Appellant's Closing Submissions) that Mr. Hahn had provided credible, uncontradicted oral testimony regarding what work his staff performed, why they performed it, what they knew at the time, what competitors were doing, and what knowledge existed in the public domain. Jentel argued that this uncontradicted testimony established a prima facie case that Jentel was attempting technological advancements, thereby demolishing the Minister's assumptions and shifting the onus to the Minister, such that if the Minister adduced no evidence to rebut that case, Jentel would be entitled to succeed.

Both Justice D'Arcy at the TCC (at paragraphs 27–28) and Justice Layden-Stevenson at the FCA (at paragraphs 4 and 7) rejected this argument, although Justice D'Arcy expressly declined to discuss its legal merits, holding instead that it failed because Jentel had not established a prima facie case that it was attempting technological advancement. The Courts held that uncontradicted lay testimony from a corporate officer does not establish a prima facie case if the substance of that very testimony describes routine engineering. As the FCA highlighted, it was precisely on the basis of Mr. Hahn's own testimony that the trial judge determined Jentel's work merely involved using existing manufacturing processes and known materials to build a better product while controlling manufacturing costs. Furthermore, Multi-Bins was Jentel's own proprietary product, distinct from its custom work for third parties; the work relied on well-known, pre-existing thermoforming and injection-moulding processes (which, as the FCA noted, Jentel had used before fiscal 2005) and on existing materials, and neither party called an independent expert witness, so the Court was left with the SAF and Mr. Hahn's own description of the work, which it found did not establish that Jentel had crossed the threshold from routine product development into experimental development.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261; aff'd 2011 FCA 355) against the specific deficiencies in the taxpayer's claim and the governing judicial standard of proof established by the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal.

headers: Judicial Standard of Proof Established by the Court

cells: Statutory Purpose: Experimental Development
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1), definition of "SR&ED", para. (c).
The taxpayer undertook a commercial product overhaul to make Multi-Bins lighter, smaller, modular, and cheaper to manufacture and ship, confusing product improvement with technological advancement.

Work must be undertaken specifically for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement in science or technology, not merely improving commercial functionality or reducing manufacturing costs using existing processes.
Criterion 1: Technological Risk or Uncertainty
Northwest Hydraulic (1998 TCC); C.W. Agencies (2001 FCA 393, para. 17).

Framed 5 commercial design targets (100 lb load, 20 cu. ft. density, snap-fit, modularity, switching ABS to polypropylene) as uncertainties. Mr. Hahn stated that the so-called "heat sink" was merely plug-assist forming technology that had "been out there for quite some time"; the Court found no evidence that any of the work involved technological risk or uncertainty.

The claimant must prove a system-level or technological barrier that cannot be resolved by "routine engineering or standard procedures" (techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field).
Criterion 2: Formulation of Scientific Hypotheses
Northwest Hydraulic; C.W. Agencies (para. 17).

The Court made no separate finding on this criterion because its finding on Criterion 1 was dispositive (2011 FCA 355, para. 6); the recorded work consisted of design and material iterations (8 plastics, 4 stand materials, 3 moulds of different casting materials, various slider shapes) that the Court characterized as the use of existing processes and materials to build a better product.

Hypotheses must be specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating a defined technological uncertainty by proposing a testable causal relationship between scientific/engineering variables, not mere material screening.
Criterion 3: Total Discipline of the Scientific Method
Northwest Hydraulic; C.W. Agencies (para. 17).

Although the SAF stipulated that the Bin Front and Back Panel tests and the Stand tests were done in a "systematic manner," the Court made no separate finding on this criterion; its decision rested on the absence of evidence of technological risk or uncertainty and of an attempt to achieve technological advancement.

A systematic procedure must accord with the total discipline of the scientific method—formulating, testing, and modifying hypotheses through rigorous experiment or analysis to explain why a technical phenomenon occurs.
Criterion 4: Technological Advancement
Northwest Hydraulic; C.W. Agencies (para. 17); Jentel (2011 FCA 355, para. 9).

The Court found no evidence of an attempt to achieve a technological advancement (para. 22) and no prima facie case that the work was undertaken for that purpose (paras. 27–28); the FCA added that the measurable objectives were pursued through routine engineering rather than true technological advance (2011 FCA 355, para. 9).

The investigation must seek to generate new technological knowledge that advances the underlying baseline of technology (including incremental technological improvements) beyond standard industry practice.
Criterion 5: Contemporaneous Documentation
Northwest Hydraulic; C.W. Agencies (para. 17); 116736 Canada Inc. (1998 TCC).

The SAF stipulated that "contemporaneous records of this work were kept" for all four work areas; the Court made no finding that record-keeping was deficient, but those records could not cure the absence of technological risk or uncertainty.

While not an absolute statutory precondition in isolation, detailed records of hypotheses tested and results kept as work progressed are essential evidentiary proof to distinguish SR&ED from routine shop-floor trial and error.
Evidentiary Burden & Prima Facie Case
Hickman Motors Ltd. v. Canada, [1997] 2 S.C.R. 336 (paras. 92–94).

Asserted that the company president's testimony about the work performed, why it was done, what was known at the time, what competitors were doing, and what knowledge was in the public domain established a prima facie case that demolished the Minister's assumptions and shifted the onus to the Minister.

The Court held that the argument failed because the evidence (the SAF and Mr. Hahn's testimony) demonstrated routine engineering and standard procedures and did not establish a prima facie case that the work was undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement; lay testimony that itself describes routine engineering cannot demolish the Minister's assumptions.
Expert vs. Fact Witness Testimony
Jentel (2011 TCC 261, para. 3); contrasted in Abeilles (2014 TCC 313).

Neither party called an independent qualified expert witness. The Court placed no weight on the CRA RTA's testimony because most of it was opinion evidence, while the Appellant relied on the SAF and its owner's testimony.

Jentel did not hold that expert evidence is required; it held only that the RTA's largely opinion-based testimony would receive no weight. In practice, fact witnesses (corporate officers or CRA RTAs) generally testify to facts they observed, and independent expert evidence can be valuable for establishing the industry "state of technology" and mapping complex facts to the 5 criteria.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers and their advisors can proactively overcome the legal and evidentiary obstacles established in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic technical projects that mirror the exact pitfalls of the 2011 ruling. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step restructuring protocol across project governance, technical documentation, contractual architecture, and experimentation tracking to satisfy subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the Northwest Hydraulic criteria.
Case Study 1: Advanced Polymer Thermoforming & Recyclable Bio-Composite Structural Packaging
Industry Scenario and the Jentel Pitfall

An Ontario-based industrial plastics manufacturer ("OntarioPlast Inc.") designs and manufactures heavy-duty reusable modular logistics totes for automotive powertrain components. Historically, OntarioPlast thermoformed these totes using virgin high-impact Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) with bolted steel corner brackets. Driven by OEM sustainability mandates and freight weight reduction targets, OntarioPlast initiates a project to replace virgin ABS and steel fasteners with a 100% recyclable, post-industrial recycled polypropylene (rPP) sheet incorporating a thermoformed "snap-fit" interlocking wall joint capable of withstanding a 150-pound dynamic stacking load while doubling volumetric packing efficiency.

On the shop floor, the engineering team orders eight different commercial grades of rPP and polyethylene sheets of varying gauges from external resin extruders. When forming the deep-draw tote walls and snap-fit undercuts, the rPP sheets suffer severe thermal sag during heating and excessive post-moulding warpage, causing the snap-fit joints to pop open under load. To fix this, operators attach standard water-cooled aluminum heat sinks (chill plugs) to the mould and test three different cast-aluminum and epoxy mould geometries. Every attempt to mould an integrated internal divider groove fails due to webbing and thin-wall tearing. If claimed in this manner, the claim would be at serious risk of disallowance by the CRA and the Tax Court of Canada under Jentel as routine material screening, parametric machine adjustment, and standard product development aimed at cost and weight reduction.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Baseline Due Diligence

To survive scrutiny under Jentel, OntarioPlast must restructure its project governance prior to commencing shop-floor trials so that commercial product goals are strictly separated from the underlying polymer science investigation. Instead of initiating a broad "Multi-Bin Product Overhaul" project, the company must institute a formal SR&ED Stage-Gate Governance Charter.

Under this governance protocol, Phase I (Routine Engineering—Excluded from SR&ED) encompasses CAD geometric design for modularity, baseline finite element analysis (FEA) using published resin datasheets, sourcing standard resin sheets, and routine machine setup. Phase II (Experimental Development—Claimed as SR&ED) is triggered only when Phase I due diligence proves that competent professionals using standard thermoforming procedures cannot resolve a fundamental technological conflict. Specifically, OntarioPlast must conduct and document a formal Literature and Patent Search, alongside written technical inquiries to its resin compounders and thermoforming machinery OEMs. This baseline dossier establishes that while virgin ABS is amorphous with high melt strength, high-crystallinity recycled polypropylene (rPP) exhibits heterogeneous molecular weight distribution (chain scission from prior recycling), causing a sharp drop in zero-shear viscosity within 5 °C of its crystalline melting point (Tm ≈ 165 °C) and severe anisotropic crystalline shrinkage (1.5–2.5%) during cooling. When standard plug-assist and heat sink procedures are applied to form a high-aspect-ratio snap-fit undercut in thick-gauge rPP, rapid localized quenching induces internal residual stress gradients that degrade the flexural modulus below the threshold required to prevent viscoelastic creep under a 150-pound load. Furthermore, governance protocols must mandate retaining an independent external polymer rheologist (such as an adjunct professor of chemical engineering) at project inception to review the baseline literature search, ensuring an independent expert is available to testify if the claim proceeds to the Tax Court of Canada.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation and Hypothesis Formulation

Rather than logging shop-floor runs across eight arbitrary plastic sheets (regarding which Justice D'Arcy stated in Jentel at paragraph 24 that he failed to see how the use of different types of plastic resin or materials constituted SR&ED), OntarioPlast must restrict its SR&ED documentation to a single, rigorously defined Technological Uncertainty and explicit, causal Scientific Hypotheses. Specifically, the technological uncertainty is formally documented in the project charter as whether high-molecular-weight disparity in post-industrial rPP sheet can be thermoformed into a high-undercut snap-fit geometry and narrow-radius retention groove without inducing localized biaxial strain-thinning or differential spherulitic crystallization that causes premature viscoelastic stress-cracking under sustained structural loads, given that standard thermoforming heat sinks and plug-assist profiles cause premature skin freezing that prevents uniform wall-thickness distribution.

To address this uncertainty, the engineering team must formulate and contemporaneously record testable hypotheses prior to each experimental campaign. Under its first primary hypothesis regarding rheological melt-sag and strain hardening, the team posits that introducing a specific bimodal long-chain branching (LCB) reactive modifier (0.5–1.0 wt%) combined with a non-linear infrared zone-heating gradient focused on the snap-fit hinge axis will induce transient extensional strain-hardening during vacuum draw, preventing wall-thinning below the critical structural threshold without exceeding the thermal degradation ceiling of the recycled polypropylene matrix. Under its second primary hypothesis governing crystalline morphology and groove forming, the team posits that replacing standard isotropic aluminum heat sinks with a selectively insulated, variable-diffusivity syntactic foam and beryllium-copper composite articulated plug will modulate the local conductive cooling rate (dT/dt) across the divider groove radius between 10 °C/s and 30 °C/s, suppressing large α-spherulite growth in favour of a fine β-crystalline nucleated microstructure that eliminates post-moulding warpage and groove collapse.
Step 3: Restructuring Contractual and Commercial Terms

In Jentel, the Appellant operated both as a custom thermoformer for third parties and as a developer of proprietary products, and specified the required gauge, size, and type of plastic sheet to be produced by third-party extruders. To prevent the CRA from arguing either that the technological baseline rested with upstream resin suppliers or that downstream customer orders funded the R&D (which triggers reductions for contract payments, as defined in subsection 127(9), under subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the Act), OntarioPlast must restructure its commercial contracts across both upstream and downstream relationships.

With respect to upstream resin extruders and tooling vendors, standard purchase orders for plastic sheet or mould castings imply routine commercial procurement. Consequently, OntarioPlast must execute custom Experimental Tolling and Material Formulation Agreements with its sheet extruder and mould foundry. These agreements must explicitly state that OntarioPlast retains full technical direction, specifies custom non-standard masterbatch additives and experimental mould thermodynamics, bears 100% of the financial risk of ruined production batches, and retains exclusive Intellectual Property (IP) ownership over all resulting processing data and tooling designs. Obtaining written technical disclaimers from the extruder stating that the custom rPP formulation falls outside standard industry warranties serves as powerful documentary proof of Criterion 1 (Technological Uncertainty). Conversely, with respect to downstream customer contracts, if an automotive OEM customer has requested the lighter totes, OntarioPlast must ensure the commercial contract is strictly a Standard Supply Agreement for Goods (transferring title only to certified commercial totes at a fixed unit price) rather than an engineering development contract. The contract must explicitly stipulate that any underlying polymer processing R&D is conducted strictly on OntarioPlast's own account, at its sole financial risk, with zero milestone payments or reimbursements for engineering, prototyping, or failed tooling trials.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking and Analytical Metrics

To avoid the Jentel SAF trap—where systematic testing was acknowledged by the Crown but dismissed by the Court as systematic routine testing—OntarioPlast must replace pass/fail load tests and visual observations ("none of the sliders worked satisfactorily") with quantitative, variable-isolated experimental matrices. Every trial run must be logged in a centralized Electronic Laboratory Notebook (ELN) tied directly to employee time-tracking codes segregated between routine shop-floor prep and eligible experimental runs.

When a divider groove or snap-fit trial fails, the engineering team must not simply try another shape. They must perform quantitative root-cause analysis—such as Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) to measure percent crystallinity (Xc), ultrasonic cross-sectional wall-thickness mapping, and tensile creep-rupture curves—and record how those analytical findings dictated the mathematical modification of the next hypothesis.

cells: Problem Definition (Criterion 1)
Defined as 5 commercial goals: 20 cu. ft. capacity, 100 lb load, snap-fit, modularity, and switching ABS to polypropylene.
Defined as overcoming the thermodynamic and rheological conflict between low melt-strength/high crystalline shrinkage in recycled PP and deep-draw undercut forming limits.
Material & Tooling Trials (Criteria 2 & 3)

Tested 8 different plastics (PETG, PVC, ABS, HDPE, etc.), 4 stand materials, and 3 moulds of different casting materials in work the SAF described as systematic (for the panels and stands) but that the Court found to be routine engineering.
Restricted trials to controlled variations of LCB-modified rPP and variable-diffusivity composite plugs governed by formal thermodynamic hypotheses.
Use of "Heat Sinks" (Criterion 1)
Used a so-called "heat sink" that Mr. Hahn described as plug-assist forming technology that had "been out there for quite some time".
Documented why standard conductive heat sinks failed (causing premature skin freeze) and engineered a novel, selectively insulated composite thermal-gradient plug.
Analysis of Failed Trials (Criteria 3 & 4)
Noted simply that "none of the sliders worked satisfactorily" and all 3 divider groove moulds failed to manufacture consistently.
Quantified why each failure occurred via DSC crystallinity assays, optical strain mapping, and viscoelastic creep equations, generating new polymer processing knowledge.

body.text: Case Study 2: Custom Industrial Automation & Multi-Material Precision Moulding System
Industry Scenario and the Jentel Pitfall

An Alberta-based industrial equipment manufacturer ("AlbertaFab Ltd.") manufactures custom material-handling assemblies for third-party agricultural and energy clients alongside its own line of automated modular storage carousels. In the current fiscal year, AlbertaFab seeks to overhaul the mechanical actuation and structural frame of its storage carousel to cut manufacturing labour by 40%, reduce structural frame weight by 50%, and eliminate welded joints. The engineering team divides the work into two areas: (1) testing structural frames made of steel, aluminum, carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer (CFRP), and timber-plastic hybrids under static load tests; and (2) designing a high-speed cam-slider and precision-moulded elastomeric guide track using three different casting alloys to eliminate mechanical fasteners.

During shop-floor testing, load tests quickly confirm that aluminum is the most cost-effective frame material. Meanwhile, over twenty iterations of cam-slider profiles jam during cycling, and all three mould castings fail to form a consistent retaining groove in the elastomeric guide track. At audit and objection, AlbertaFab relies on the oral testimony of its founder—who states that no competitor in Alberta builds a snap-together carousel like this and that the work was done systematically to build a better product while controlling manufacturing costs. Under Jentel (2011 TCC 261; 2011 FCA 355), this claim would be highly vulnerable: the frame material comparison is routine structural engineering, the slider/mould iterations are unguided mechanical trial-and-error, and the founder's testimony actively proves that the company merely used existing processes to build a better commercial product while controlling costs.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Baseline Due Diligence

AlbertaFab must immediately overhaul its internal project selection and claim preparation governance to excise routine engineering before a claim is ever filed with the CRA. First, under the Jentel standard, the comparative testing of steel, aluminum, CFRP, and hybrid frames against defined load criteria must be completely carved out and excluded from the SR&ED claim. Because calculating moments of inertia, yield strength, and Euler buckling loads across known structural materials is textbook mechanical engineering accessible to any competent professional, including it in the T661 claim taints the credibility of the entire submission.

Second, for the cam-slider and precision-moulded guide track, AlbertaFab must establish an Engineering Review Board (ERB) prior to fabrication. The ERB must compile a Baseline State-of-Technology Report documenting why standard mechanical design rules (such as Shigley's mechanical engineering kinematics, standard Tribology friction tables, and published ASME mould-shrinkage tolerances) cannot predict or resolve the failure of the slider-groove interface. Specifically, the governance dossier must demonstrate that when coupling a high-speed metallic cam-slider directly into a thin-walled, snap-in elastomeric/thermoplastic hybrid guide groove without mechanical fasteners, dynamic frictional heating at cycle rates exceeding 120 cycles per minute induces a localized glass-transition softening (Tg shift) and stick-slip acoustic resonance at the groove undercut. Furthermore, when attempting to cast the complex micro-textured mould required to form this self-lubricating groove, differential thermal contraction across the casting alloy interface causes micro-fissures and dimensional distortion exceeding the kinematic clearance limit.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation and Hypothesis Formulation

To prevent the Tax Court from concluding that trying "many various shapes and forms of sliders" and "3 different moulds, each made of different casting materials" is merely routine engineering and standard procedures (as the Court concluded with respect to the work described in Jentel, SAF paragraphs 13–14), AlbertaFab must reframe its technical documentation around causal physical mechanisms and mathematical hypotheses. With respect to tribology and dynamic kinematics, the engineering documentation must articulate the core technological uncertainty as whether a fastener-free, snap-in polymeric guide groove can maintain structural retention and low-friction kinematic sliding under high-frequency eccentric cam loading (≥2 Hz) without undergoing thermo-viscoelastic stick-slip seizure or undercut shear fatigue, given that standard clearance tolerances and surface finishes either permit cam derailment or induce rapid thermal seizure. Concurrently, regarding mould casting metallurgy, the secondary technological uncertainty is defined as whether a bi-metallic casting mould can be solidified to form a high-aspect-ratio micro-ribbed groove profile without inducing dendritic shrinkage porosity or interfacial thermal-expansion delamination at the groove root during cyclical thermal moulding.

Rather than documenting that the team "designed and tested many various shapes of sliders," AlbertaFab must record explicit scientific hypotheses prior to fabrication. Under Hypothesis A, the team postulates that machining an asymmetric involute slider profile coupled with a micro-cavitation sinusoidal relief pattern (50 µm depth) into the moulded groove wall will disrupt the continuous boundary-layer contact patch, reducing localized flash temperature at the cam-groove interface by 30 °C and eliminating stick-slip resonance without compromising the lateral pull-out retention force. Under Hypothesis B, the team postulates that applying directional solidification via controlled silicon-carbide chill inserts within a beryllium-modified aluminum-bronze casting mould will suppress dendritic porosity at the groove root and stabilize dimensional tolerance within ±0.05 mm over 10,000 thermal cycles.
Step 3: Restructuring Contractual and Commercial Terms

Because AlbertaFab performs custom fabrication for third-party industrial clients alongside its proprietary product lines (mirroring Jentel's exact business model described at paragraph 4 of the TCC ruling), it faces severe contractual and evidentiary exposure. If shop-floor personnel work on both custom client orders and the proprietary carousel project without strict contractual and accounting segregation, the CRA will challenge the expenditure pool and argue that the work was routine custom engineering performed to fulfill commercial client orders.

To neutralize this vulnerability, AlbertaFab must implement a three-tier contractual and evidentiary protocol. First, regarding work-order and cost-accounting segregation, management must establish dedicated internal Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) codes that ring-fence all engineering labour, machine shop time, and sacrificial prototype materials dedicated to Hypotheses A and B from commercial shop-floor orders. Second, when deploying failed or experimental slider-groove prototypes at a customer facility for high-cycle testing, AlbertaFab must execute a formal No-Charge Experimental Field Trial Agreement specifying that the prototype unit remains the legal property of AlbertaFab, is installed strictly to gather telemetry data under real-world boundary conditions, carries no commercial performance warranty, and must be returned or scrapped upon completion of the test matrix. Third, learning directly from the Hickman Motors failure in Jentel, AlbertaFab's tax litigation counsel must ensure that in the event of a dispute, the company does not rely solely on its business owner's lay narrative about "building a better product while controlling manufacturing costs". Instead, the company must retain an independent Ph.D. mechanical and metallurgical engineer under Rule 145 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) to author an independent Expert Report that maps every experimental iteration directly to the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, while preparing internal engineering leads to testify strictly on the scientific hypotheses and quantitative failure data.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking and Analytical Metrics

In Jentel, the fact that none of the sliders worked satisfactorily and every divider groove attempt failed did not save the claim, because the Court found no evidence that any of the work involved technological risk or uncertainty or was an attempt to achieve technological advancement; nothing in the evidence showed how the failures advanced technological knowledge. Under subsection 248(1) of the Act and the Northwest Hydraulic doctrine, a project whose physical prototypes fail completely can still be eligible for SR&ED tax credits provided the systematic testing and analysis yield a technological advancement—namely, new scientific or engineering knowledge proving why a specific technological approach will not work within given physical laws.

To capture this advancement, AlbertaFab must institute a quantitative Experimental Failure & Advancement Ledger. Every iteration of the slider and casting mould must be instrumented and tracked against physical parameters rather than visual pass/fail inspection:

headers: Quantitative Analytical Conclusion & Modification of Hypothesis (Technological Advancement)

cells: Trial Series 1.1–1.4 (Slider Kinematics)
Cam-slider contact radius (2 mm to 8 mm) and groove undercut angle (15° to 45°).
Infrared thermography of interface flash temperature (°C); laser vibrometry stick-slip amplitude (µm); dynamic coefficient of friction (μk).

At a 2 mm contact radius, normal contact stress exceeds 35 MPa, causing localized flash temperature to reach 140 °C within 90 seconds, triggering viscoelastic shear seizure. Hypothesis modified to introduce sinusoidal micro-relief grooves to decouple normal retention force from sliding contact area.
Trial Series 2.1–2.3 (Mould Metallurgy)
Casting alloy composition (Al-Si-Mg vs. Cu-Al-Be) and local SiC chill thermal conductivity (W/m·K).
Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) secondary dendrite arm spacing (λ₂ in µm); Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM) groove profile deviation (mm).

Proved that standard gravity casting of Al-Si-Mg induces a 60 µm SDAS porosity zone at the sharp groove root due to convergent heat flux. Directional solidification via Cu-Al-Be with targeted SiC chills reduced SDAS to 20 µm and held groove geometry within ±0.05 mm, resolving the moulding uncertainty.

body.text: 5. Strategic Synthesis and Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The rulings of the Tax Court of Canada (2011 TCC 261) and the Federal Court of Appeal (2011 FCA 355) in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen establish three enduring legal imperatives for Canadian corporate taxpayers, technical R&D directors, and tax counsel navigating the SR&ED program.

First, systematic methodology and contemporaneous records cannot cure the absence of technological uncertainty. A taxpayer may conduct dozens of structured physical trials across multiple materials, maintain meticulous shop-floor logs, and even secure a formal stipulation from the Crown in a Statement of Agreed Facts that the work was systematic and contemporaneously recorded, yet still face total disallowance if the underlying problem can be resolved through techniques, procedures, and data accessible to competent professionals in the field. Comparative material screening (testing eight commercial plastic resins or four structural stand materials) and deploying known industry techniques (such as the so-called "heat sink," which was merely plug-assist forming technology) must be rigorously segregated from eligible experimental development.

Second, product performance objectives and manufacturing cost-control targets must never be pleaded as technological uncertainties. While the Income Tax Act explicitly recognizes incremental improvements to existing products and processes under paragraph (c) of the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED, the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in Jentel that the improvement sought must be an incremental technological advancement, not merely a functional or commercial improvement achieved through routine engineering. Technical narratives must articulate the exact scientific, thermodynamic, rheological, or mechanical system constraints that prevent standard engineering procedures from achieving the desired outcome.

Third, litigation strategy before the Tax Court of Canada requires objective scientific proof and independent expert validation rather than reliance on Hickman Motors burden-shifting technicalities. The Court's decision to place no weight on the CRA RTA's opinion testimony does not assist an appellant if the appellant's own lay witnesses describe their work in commercial terms that confirm the Minister's assumption of routine engineering. By embedding baseline state-of-technology literature searches, causal hypothesis formulation, quantitative root-cause failure analytics, and independent expert oversight directly into R&D project governance, Canadian manufacturers can decisively cross the evidentiary threshold required by Northwest Hydraulic and Jentel.

outcome: Order/ruling issued; court addressed procedural and evidentiary issues prior to the subsequent 2011 TCC decision.
